title: Corporate Crush

jokes.text: Your face... it's like you're happy or something.
jokes.setup: Frank notices something unusual about Liz's expression.
jokes.punchline: He identifies happiness as the strange, almost alarming thing he's seeing — as if it's aberrant.
jokes.explanation: Quick, efficient joke establishing that Liz's baseline is misery. Frank's delivery of happiness as something 'wrong' is a nice character beat. Competent but not exceptional.

jokes.text: 'Cause of that dude you're donking.
jokes.setup: Frank asks why Liz is happy.
jokes.punchline: He uses the made-up slang 'donking' for sex, which is both crude and oddly innocent.
jokes.explanation: 'Donking' is a great invented word — sounds gross but not overtly vulgar, perfectly Frank. High economy, strong character integration. The invented slang is the show at its quick-fire best.

jokes.text: Frank attempts to point out something on Liz's face — 'Right here? Other side. Here? Up a little. In that area? You got it.' — and the interaction has no payoff because the audience never learns what it was.
jokes.setup: Frank says Liz has something on her face and attempts to direct her to it.
jokes.punchline: The bit escalates in time and intimacy ('up a little, in that area') with no resolution, the comedy coming from the absurd investment in something trivial.
jokes.explanation: A slight physical comedy bit that works as filler. The escalating vagueness ('in that area') is a mild comic rhythm but doesn't land a real punchline.

jokes.text: Oh, that movie was a complete waste of time. / I thought it was moving... my bowels.
jokes.setup: One writer says the movie was a waste of time; another starts to defend it with 'I thought it was moving...'
jokes.punchline: '...my bowels.' — a classic misdirect from heartfelt to scatological.
jokes.explanation: Textbook misdirect, extremely well-structured. The pause after 'moving' does the heavy lifting. Economy is excellent. Loses points on originality and character integration — it's a classic joke form that could work in any show, but the execution here is crisp.

jokes.text: Reverse, Reverse, Skip, Skip, Draw Four!
jokes.setup: Cut to a writer's room scene with no context.
jokes.punchline: Someone shouts Uno card commands — suggesting a chaotic Uno game is happening in the writers' room during work hours.
jokes.explanation: A quick absurdist beat that perfectly characterizes the TGS writers' room as professionally unserious. The commitment and brevity are the joke. High economy score — five words do everything.

jokes.text: Frank offers to come over and videotape Liz and Floyd 'doing it or whatever' and says 'I can make room in my schedule.'
jokes.setup: Frank says he's happy for Liz that she found someone, framing it sincerely.
jokes.punchline: He undermines the sweet sentiment by offering to film them having sex — then adds 'No judgments.' as a capper.
jokes.explanation: Three-beat joke: sweet setup, pervy pivot, 'No judgments' topper. Frank's sleazy-but-genuine quality is perfectly captured. 'I can make room in my schedule' treats this as a calendar obligation, which escalates the absurdity. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: I got a welt on my ass the size of a Red Delicious apple.
jokes.setup: Geiss explains he can't sit down because he was stung by a jellyfish snorkeling at St. Barts.
jokes.punchline: The overly specific fruit comparison ('Red Delicious apple') for a butt welt is the joke — the wealthy absurdity of the detail (St. Barts, snorkeling with grandkids) compounds it.
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'Red Delicious' (not just 'apple') is the key comedic choice — it's the kind of precise-yet-absurd detail 30 Rock excels at. Also sets up why Geiss is standing throughout the scene, giving the visual gag a practical payoff.

jokes.text: 'If you try, you win.' / 'And he was a hell of a garbageman.'
jokes.setup: Geiss quotes his father's motivational wisdom: 'If you try, you win.'
jokes.punchline: Immediate deflation — his father was a garbageman, making the grand wisdom feel hilariously small-stakes and specific.
jokes.explanation: Near-perfect joke structure. The wisdom sounds profound, and the single-sentence deflation ('And he was a hell of a garbageman') recontextualizes it entirely. The beat between the quote and the follow-up, implied by the timestamp gap, is where the comedy lives. Great economy — nine words do everything the punchline needs.

jokes.text: But I'm taking the Microwave Division away from you.
jokes.setup: Geiss says warmly that everyone still has a lot of faith in Jack.
jokes.punchline: Immediately undercuts it by removing his Microwave Division — delivered as a casual afterthought.
jokes.explanation: Classic 30 Rock structural whiplash — build up a character only to immediately undercut them. The casual delivery makes it land harder. The joke also absurdly treats 'Microwave Division' as a serious thing to lose, which is its own running comedic premise.

jokes.text: Well, look at Bob. His wife looks just like Walter Matthau, but she's always there for him.
jokes.setup: Geiss encourages Jack to get remarried, noting everyone in the division is married.
jokes.punchline: His example of a good marriage is a woman who looks like Walter Matthau — but Geiss presents this as a compliment to the arrangement.
jokes.explanation: The specific celebrity choice (Walter Matthau) is inspired — he's both a very specific face and distinctly unglamorous. Geiss delivering this as sincere relationship advice reveals his entire worldview: loyalty over beauty, function over pleasure. Great character integration for a secondary character.

jokes.text: What's that film where he turned into a dog? / 'Fat Bitch,' sir. / That's it. I love it. / Boy, that's a great film.
jokes.setup: Geiss says he's going to see Tracy Jordan and can't remember the film title.
jokes.punchline: 'Fat Bitch' — the film title is inherently absurd, and Geiss's sincere enthusiasm ('Boy, that's a great film') treats it as a prestige picture.
jokes.explanation: The joke works on two levels: the inherently funny film title, and the powerful executive speaking about 'Fat Bitch' with the reverence of a Spielberg film. Jack's deadpan delivery of the title to his boss elevates the moment. Sets up callbacks later in the episode.

jokes.text: Jack looks at himself in the mirror/reflective surface and says 'I'm sorry I let you down.'
jokes.setup: After being demoted and lectured by Geiss, Jack is alone.
jokes.punchline: He appears to be apologizing to himself — his own reflection — which is both pathetic and grandiose in a Jack-specific way.
jokes.explanation: Four words that perfectly encapsulate Jack's massive ego — his version of self-pity is apologizing to himself as if he is his own disappointed superior. Strong character integration for a brief beat.

jokes.text: I call it 'Jefferson.' / A movie version of 'The Jeffersons'? / I love it. / No, Thomas Jefferson.
jokes.setup: Tracy pitches his movie 'Jefferson' to Don Geiss, who immediately assumes it's a Jeffersons TV adaptation.
jokes.punchline: It's actually about Thomas Jefferson — which turns out to be even more absurd.
jokes.explanation: A double misdirect: the audience also assumes 'Jeffersons' before the correction, and then the 'true' answer (Thomas Jefferson) is equally absurd. The structure is tight. Geiss's immediate enthusiasm for the TV adaptation is a good character beat too.

jokes.text: I just recently found out that he went to town on one of my ancestors, so we're related.
jokes.setup: Tracy explains why he's passionate about the Thomas Jefferson project.
jokes.punchline: His connection to Jefferson is through Jefferson's documented sexual relationship with his slave Sally Hemings — described with the euphemism 'went to town on,' making it both historically pointed and absurdly casual.
jokes.explanation: A rare moment where Tracy's absurdism grounds in actual historical fact (the Jefferson-Hemings relationship), making it both pointed social commentary and comedy. The euphemism 'went to town on' is well-chosen — casual enough to be funny, clear enough to land.

jokes.text: You want to play Thomas Jefferson? / And Sally Hemings and King George. I'm gonna play all the parts.
jokes.setup: Tracy confirms he wants to star in the Jefferson movie.
jokes.punchline: He's not just playing Jefferson — he's playing ALL the parts, including a British king and a slave.
jokes.explanation: A beautifully escalating absurdist joke. Each additional role Tracy claims (Sally Hemings, King George) escalates both the comedic and thematic absurdity. The list structure rewards the audience for waiting. Strong character work — only Tracy Jordan would approach history this way. Quotable and memorable.

jokes.text: Did you know he had a lisp? / What's up, stupid jerks? I'm Thomas Jefferson.
jokes.setup: Tracy claims Thomas Jefferson had a lisp.
jokes.punchline: He immediately demonstrates his Jefferson impression — which sounds nothing like a Founding Father and everything like Tracy Jordan.
jokes.explanation: 'What's up, stupid jerks? I'm Thomas Jefferson.' is a genuinely great comedy line. The impression sounds exactly like Tracy talking in his normal register, making the claimed lisp a total non-sequitur. High character integration — this could only be Tracy. Quotable.

jokes.text: So we gonna need about $35 million to do this thing right. I'm gonna get us one of those big clocks, and I'm gonna hang it in there.
jokes.setup: Tracy wraps up his pitch to Don Geiss.
jokes.punchline: His entire $35 million budget plan is apparently a big clock ('one of those big clocks'), which is both hilariously vague and historically disconnected.
jokes.explanation: Tracy's pitch ending on 'a big clock' perfectly characterizes his unfocused grandiosity. The vagueness ('one of those big clocks') is funnier than any specific clock would be. Good character comedy but not a standout punchline.

jokes.text: Aw, Lutz, that's okay. I'm just glad you're here. / Aw, you got a face like a baby's bottom. / Poop!
jokes.setup: Liz is in such a good mood she's being uncharacteristically sweet to Lutz, who arrives late.
jokes.punchline: She compliments him with 'face like a baby's bottom' — then Lutz immediately takes it to its logical (scatological) conclusion: 'Poop!'
jokes.explanation: Two-step joke: the setup (Liz being sweet) is already funny given her character, and Lutz completing the baby metaphor with 'Poop!' is a perfectly timed childish punctuation. Shows both characters well in two lines.

jokes.text: I hate when you're in a good mood. It makes me feel unsafe, like when my mom used to make daiquiris and sing Tanya Tucker songs.
jokes.setup: A writer reacts to Liz's uncharacteristic happiness.
jokes.punchline: The writer's unease escalates to a specific traumatic childhood memory — mom's daiquiris and Tanya Tucker songs as a harbinger of disaster.
jokes.explanation: The specificity is the joke here — not just 'when my mom was drunk' but the exact cultural markers (daiquiris, Tanya Tucker). This transforms a reaction beat into a surprisingly rich, darkly funny character detail. The response — 'That sounds awesome' — also works as a topper.

jokes.text: That sounds awesome. [in response to mom making daiquiris and singing Tanya Tucker]
jokes.setup: Writer describes their traumatic association with Liz's good mood.
jokes.punchline: Liz, in her good-mood bubble, genuinely finds it appealing.
jokes.explanation: Quick topper that pays off the previous joke. Liz's oblivious positivity is perfectly encapsulated in three words. Good economy but dependent on the setup joke.

jokes.text: Jack goes to Sbarro when he's angry, the New York Stock Exchange when he's horny, and Christie's auction house when he's depressed.
jokes.setup: Jonathan tells Liz that Jack is across the street at Christie's.
jokes.punchline: He reveals he has a detailed map of Jack's emotional states keyed to specific New York locations — presented matter-of-factly.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. Three-part structure with perfectly escalating absurdity: Sbarro (funny chain restaurant choice), New York Stock Exchange (horny→financial power is inspired), Christie's (depression→art acquisition). Each destination reveals something about Jack's character and Jonathan's obsessive knowledge of him. It's a triple punchline with perfect internal logic. The Stock Exchange is the peak. Highly quotable, strong rewatch value.

jokes.text: You've been avoiding me, Lemon. / How do you do that without turning around?
jokes.setup: Jack somehow identifies Liz entering Christie's without turning around.
jokes.punchline: Liz is impressed/unsettled enough to ask how he does it, implying this is a genuine sixth sense.
jokes.explanation: A nice character beat establishing Jack's predatory/perceptive nature. The question 'How do you do that without turning around?' treats it as a legitimate supernatural ability, which is funnier than if the show explained it.

jokes.text: To be perfectly honest, the first couple of people I did that to were not you, but... here we are.
jokes.setup: Jack responds to Liz's question about how he knew it was her without turning around.
jokes.punchline: He essentially admits he guessed and got lucky after a few misses — delivered with complete aplomb.
jokes.explanation: Excellent joke. Sets up Jack as seemingly all-knowing, then reveals he's been doing 'cold reads' of random people and got lucky. 'But... here we are' is a masterclass in character-specific economy — it captures Jack's ability to reframe any failure as a reasonable outcome. Strong character integration: only Jack would deliver this with zero embarrassment. Comparable in quality to an 8.0 anchor.

jokes.text: Those were such lovely pieces. The ruby-and-diamond cluster ring was particularly exquisite. / Yeah, that was her engagement ring.
jokes.setup: Phoebe recalls selling Jack's ex-wife's jewelry to an anonymous buyer.
jokes.punchline: One of the 'lovely pieces' was the engagement ring — sold off along with everything else, casually.
jokes.explanation: Good dark comedy beat establishing the depth of Jack's divorce bitterness. The matter-of-fact inclusion of the engagement ring in the 'lovely pieces' subverts sentiment effectively.

jokes.text: I took the money from the sale of those pieces, and I bought a sailboat. And I named it after my ex-wife, and I sank it.
jokes.setup: Jack explains what he did with the proceeds from selling his ex-wife's jewelry.
jokes.punchline: He bought a boat, named it after her, and deliberately sank it — a three-step revenge fantasy executed with chilling calm.
jokes.explanation: Three-step escalation delivered in one breath: sold jewelry → bought boat → named it → sank it. Each step is a commitment. The calmness of delivery makes it funnier and more disturbing. Strong character integration — Jack's pettiness on this scale is perfectly him. The follow-up detail ('the Bianca Blows') elevates it further.

jokes.text: It's true... the Bianca Blows is somewhere at the bottom of the Peconic Bay.
jokes.setup: Jack has just said he sank the boat he named after his ex-wife Bianca.
jokes.punchline: The boat's name, 'the Bianca Blows,' is both a maritime naming convention (ships are 'the [name]') and a crude double entendre — he named it something insulting.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. 'The Bianca Blows' works on multiple levels: the double meaning (nautical naming vs. crude insult), the specificity of 'Peconic Bay,' and Jack's absolute zero-remorse delivery. The combination of petty cruelty, wordplay, and geographic specificity is peak 30 Rock. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor — arguably better.

jokes.text: I wish I were a horse... strong, free... my chestnut haunches glistening in the sun.
jokes.setup: Jack is looking at equestrian paintings at Christie's in his depressed state.
jokes.punchline: His identification with the horse goes from poetic (strong, free) to oddly sensuous ('chestnut haunches glistening in the sun') — the specificity of 'chestnut haunches' crosses a line into comedy.
jokes.explanation: Jack's depression manifesting as horse-envy is excellent character work. 'Chestnut haunches glistening in the sun' is the punchline within the punchline — the escalation from admirable qualities (strong, free) to sensual physical detail is both funny and revealing about Jack's state of mind.

jokes.text: I'm not a creative type like you with your work sneakers and your left-handedness.
jokes.setup: Jack is apologizing for being hard on Liz about the special.
jokes.punchline: His description of 'creative type' reduces it to physical markers — work sneakers and left-handedness — as if these are the defining traits of creative people.
jokes.explanation: Jack reducing 'creative type' to 'work sneakers and left-handedness' is a beautifully specific put-down disguised as a compliment. It reveals Jack's inability to understand creativity while also being gently condescending. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: His name is Floyd. / That's unfortunate.
jokes.setup: Liz corrects Jack's reference to Floyd as 'flower guy.'
jokes.punchline: Jack's response to the name 'Floyd' is simply 'That's unfortunate' — an understated dismissal of an entire person based on their name.
jokes.explanation: Two words, maximum character. Jack's casual dismissal of Floyd purely based on his name establishes the dynamic that will drive the episode. Perfect economy. Only Jack says something this casually cruel.

jokes.text: I'd like to meet the man that made Liz Lemon shirk her responsibilities. Let's say Priscille, 9:00... be sure to wear a tie.
jokes.setup: Liz asks Jack to meet Floyd.
jokes.punchline: Jack agrees, but frames the meeting as a formal audition for Floyd ('be sure to wear a tie'), revealing he sees himself as the arbiter of Liz's personal life.
jokes.explanation: Jack treating Liz's boyfriend introduction as a corporate interview (specific restaurant, dress code) is good character comedy. Establishes the Jack-Floyd dynamic that will drive the episode.

jokes.text: Well, remember when Fat Bitch called all her dog friends together, and they used their high-pitched howling to mess... / You're right, K. I should make my own 'Jefferson' preview.
jokes.setup: Kenneth starts giving Tracy advice by referencing a plot point from 'Fat Bitch.'
jokes.punchline: Tracy cuts him off mid-sentence, deciding he's already gotten the lesson — and the lesson he takes from 'Fat Bitch' is to self-finance his movie.
jokes.explanation: Callback to 'Fat Bitch' that uses the film as a genuine source of life wisdom for Tracy, and Kenneth earnestly explaining the plot. Tracy interpreting the incomplete story as a business lesson is classic Tracy logic. The interrupted punchline ('to mess...') is also funny.

jokes.text: I'm never gonna finish this bikini before Nana's birthday.
jokes.setup: Brief cut to a writer's room scene.
jokes.punchline: A writer is inexplicably knitting a bikini as a birthday gift for their grandmother.
jokes.explanation: Perfectly constructed throwaway joke. The specificity — not just 'knitting' but knitting a bikini, not just 'a relative' but Nana — makes it. A one-liner that functions as a complete character portrait in ten words.

jokes.text: Liz Lemon, you are my Alexander Hamilton.
jokes.setup: Tracy is pitching Liz to help him with the Jefferson trailer.
jokes.punchline: He casts her as Hamilton in his Jefferson worldview — both historically confused (Hamilton and Jefferson were rivals) and oddly flattering.
jokes.explanation: Tracy's comparison works because it's both historically wrong (Hamilton was Jefferson's adversary) and reveals Tracy only has one mode: the Jefferson lens. Liz's response 'I don't know what that means' is the perfect reaction beat.

jokes.text: Jack wrote a book? / 'Jack Attack: The Art of Aggression in Business.'
jokes.setup: Floyd mentions he's read Jack's book 20 times.
jokes.punchline: The book's title, 'Jack Attack: The Art of Aggression in Business,' is an absurdly self-aggrandizing business title that also sounds like a self-help book by a Bond villain.
jokes.explanation: The title 'Jack Attack: The Art of Aggression in Business' is perfectly calibrated — sounds exactly like a book Jack would write and exactly like a book a certain type of businessman would actually read. Floyd having read it 20 times is its own joke about Floyd's character.

jokes.text: Oh, no. / He got here before us. / You're not supposed to let that happen. / That's chapter two in the book.
jokes.setup: Liz and Floyd arrive at the restaurant and see Jack already seated.
jokes.punchline: Floyd recognizes this as a dominance tactic from Jack's book ('chapter two'), revealing he's analyzed Jack academically and still lost.
jokes.explanation: Excellent callback and payoff — Floyd has studied Jack's tactics and immediately clocks being outmaneuvered. The joke that Floyd has read the book 20 times but is STILL being played by chapter two is great dramatic irony. 'That's chapter two' is very quotable.

jokes.text: The only other 'Floyd' I ever knew was this Korean barber who used to cut my hair down in the 50th Street subway station. / That's my dad. I'm Floyd Jr. / I'm just kidding.
jokes.setup: Jack passive-aggressively diminishes Floyd by associating his name with a subway barber.
jokes.punchline: Floyd claims the barber is his father, blindsiding Jack — then immediately reveals he's joking, restoring the power dynamic.
jokes.explanation: Three-beat joke with a twist and a counter-twist. Jack tries a dominance move, Floyd outmaneuvers him briefly with 'That's my dad,' creating a genuine surprise beat before revealing it's a joke. The structure is tight and it characterizes both men efficiently. Floyd demonstrating he can play Jack's game is important plot work done through comedy.

jokes.text: And 'Attack of the Clones,' which was seriously the worst of the 'Star Wars.'
jokes.setup: Floyd is earnestly listing Jack's impressive business accomplishments to Jack's face.
jokes.punchline: He interrupts his own professional eulogy with a deeply personal opinion about Star Wars — a complete tonal break inserted into a business presentation.
jokes.explanation: The sudden insertion of a Star Wars opinion into a business speech reveals Floyd's nervous-young-man character while also being a structurally surprising comedy move. The fact that Liz is clearly trying to flag him to stop makes it better.

jokes.text: In my mind, the Foo Fighters' song 'Best of You' is about your managerial skills.
jokes.setup: Floyd continues his escalating over-the-top tribute to Jack.
jokes.punchline: He claims a Foo Fighters rock song is secretly about Jack Donaghy's management abilities.
jokes.explanation: Highly original and specific. The Foo Fighters 'Best of You' is a real song that sounds vaguely inspiring, and applying it to Jack's 'managerial skills' is a delightful absurdist leap. 'In my mind' is the perfect qualifier — he's not claiming it's objectively true, just that he's made this personal connection. The earnestness sells it. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: Lemon, I want to kiss your boyfriend on the mouth.
jokes.setup: Floyd has just delivered an over-the-top tribute to Jack's accomplishments.
jokes.punchline: Jack's response — wanting to kiss Floyd on the mouth — is delivered as a completely sincere professional compliment, not romantically but as an expression of pure approval.
jokes.explanation: Jack's highest form of professional praise is wanting to kiss someone on the mouth — delivered deadpan, to Liz, about her boyfriend. The jealousy/territorial dynamic set up with Liz makes it funnier. 'On the mouth' is the specific detail that makes this memorable. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: Chapter 12. [said immediately after Jack says he wants to kiss Floyd on the mouth]
jokes.setup: Jack expresses extreme approval of Floyd.
jokes.punchline: Floyd immediately identifies Jack's behavior as a tactic from his own book — 'Chapter 12' — suggesting Jack has a chapter on expressing extreme approval.
jokes.explanation: Two words, perfect callback. The joke escalates the book bit by revealing Jack has a playbook chapter for EVERY move, including wanting to kiss someone on the mouth. Floyd flagging it in real-time as 'Chapter 12' is a brilliant power play. Maximum economy (two words) for maximum impact. The runners — 'Chapter 2' earlier, 'Chapter 12' now — create a running gag payoff.

jokes.text: What are you drinking? / Club soda. / Oh, that's a shame. Pete.
jokes.setup: Jack asks Floyd what he's drinking.
jokes.punchline: Floyd says 'club soda,' and Jack responds 'Oh, that's a shame' — expressing genuine pity at the choice — then immediately pivots to Pete as if making a transaction.
jokes.explanation: Quick character beat — Jack judges Floyd as lesser for not drinking (his world requires drinking). Calling out 'Pete' immediately after is a funny non-sequitur that implies he's going to make some kind of compensatory drink order. Good economy.

jokes.text: Hey, Liz Lemon. Could you go away for a while? I got to get rid of Freddie's erection.
jokes.setup: Tracy appears with a horse in Liz's office area.
jokes.punchline: The request to 'get rid of Freddie's erection' sounds immediately alarming before being revealed to be about a horse.
jokes.explanation: Classic misdirect — the 'erection' refers to the horse's problem, creating a moment of shock before clarification. Tracy delivering this with complete seriousness and nonchalance is perfect. Solid joke, though the form is familiar.

jokes.text: Freddie is playing the part of Thomas Jefferson's horse, Caractacus.
jokes.setup: Liz demands an explanation for the horse.
jokes.punchline: Tracy has not only brought a real horse to the office but given it a historical character name — he's fully committed to the Jefferson project at a production level that includes casting.
jokes.explanation: Good absurdist escalation of the Jefferson project — Tracy is so committed he's hired and named a horse. The specific historical-sounding name 'Caractacus' is funnier than a generic name would be. Sets up horse jokes later.

jokes.text: I don't shake hands. I have avian bone syndrome. / Hollow bones.
jokes.setup: Liz extends her hand to shake Phoebe's.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe declines due to 'avian bone syndrome' — a fake medical condition suggesting her bones are bird-like and hollow.
jokes.explanation: 'Avian bone syndrome' is an inspired fake medical condition — it sounds vaguely plausible while being completely absurd. The follow-up 'Hollow bones.' as a clarifying statement makes it better. This is the kind of specific medical absurdity 30 Rock does brilliantly, and it becomes a running gag.

jokes.text: They look just like the one crapping in my office.
jokes.setup: Jack asks Liz's opinion on equestrian paintings at Christie's.
jokes.punchline: Liz identifies them by reference to the horse currently using her office as a toilet.
jokes.explanation: Good callback that recontextualizes Jack's art appreciation. The juxtaposition of fine equestrian art and a horse actively defecating in Liz's office is well-constructed. Liz's practical perspective vs. Jack's aesthetic one is a good character contrast.

jokes.text: Don't give him a nickname before I do.
jokes.setup: Jack refers to Floyd as 'the Floydster.'
jokes.punchline: Liz's objection is not that Jack is getting too close to Floyd, but that he's jumping the nickname queue — a very Liz-specific territorial response.
jokes.explanation: Sharp character joke — Liz's issue with Jack's intimacy with Floyd is expressed through the lens of nickname ownership. The specific complaint (nickname timing) reveals her territorial, slightly childish response to a legitimate threat. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: Pray, who be this Tracy Jordan thou speakest of? / Uh, President Jefferson, we got a problem.
jokes.setup: Kenneth addresses Tracy by name on set.
jokes.punchline: Tracy is fully in character as Thomas Jefferson, denying his own name — in a fake Elizabethan accent.
jokes.explanation: Tracy staying in a Jefferson character who speaks in vaguely Shakespearean English is a good absurdist bit. Kenneth's immediate adjustment to 'President Jefferson' is perfect Kenneth behavior.

jokes.text: Pray, who be this Tracy Jordan thou speakest of? / President Jefferson, we got a problem. / Speakest.
jokes.setup: Someone interrupts Tracy while he's in character as Jefferson
jokes.punchline: Tracy is so deep in character he corrects the conjugation — 'Speakest' — while still in Jefferson voice, which is both absurd and oddly committed
jokes.explanation: Tracy correcting someone's Early Modern English conjugation while in character as Jefferson is unexpectedly brilliant — he's somehow both a committed method actor and completely ridiculous. The specificity of 'speakest' implies Tracy has studied this. Justifies 8.

jokes.text: That horse ate your wig. / Well, stand guard by his rump and await it in his droppings. / Or we could probably just go get a new wig. / Aha, I like you, young man. You shall run my university.
jokes.setup: Tracy (as Jefferson) is told his wig was eaten by the horse.
jokes.punchline: His first instinct is to wait for the wig to pass through the horse; Kenneth's practical alternative (new wig) pleases him so much he grants Kenneth stewardship of a university.
jokes.explanation: A perfectly structured four-beat escalating joke. Beat 1: absurd problem (horse ate wig). Beat 2: Tracy's insane solution (await it in droppings). Beat 3: Kenneth's sane alternative. Beat 4: Tracy rewarding practicality by immediately granting Kenneth control of a university. Each beat is funnier than the last. 'You shall run my university' is a great non-sequitur reward that stays perfectly in character. One of the episode's best jokes.

jokes.text: Yeah, yeah. No, it's very nice. / Jack bought me this painting. / Wow. / Um... is that lion eating the horse? / Or perhaps it's eating universal healthcare.
jokes.setup: Floyd shows off a painting Jack bought him. Liz asks if the lion is eating the horse.
jokes.punchline: Jack responds 'Or perhaps it's eating universal healthcare' — a non-sequitur political aside that reveals Jack's worldview (healthcare as prey to be consumed).
jokes.explanation: Exceptional character joke. 'Or perhaps it's eating universal healthcare' inserts Jack's politics into art interpretation in a way that is startlingly funny and perfectly in character. The non-sequitur quality makes it land like a slap. This could only be Jack. One of the episode's best jokes — strong originality, near-perfect character integration, excellent economy. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor.

jokes.text: It's kind of like you two are dating. [Liz reacts]
jokes.setup: Jack has bought Floyd a painting and invited himself to lunch with them.
jokes.punchline: Floyd observes the obvious — Jack and Floyd are acting like they're dating — and the camera catches Liz's reaction to this being true.
jokes.explanation: Good observation joke that names the dynamic explicitly. Floyd's phrasing is perfectly casual, making the truth of it funnier. The subsequent beat of Liz's reaction is the real punchline.

jokes.text: Um, I think that Coulter was right. [said by Liz immediately after Floyd says 'it's like you two are dating']
jokes.setup: Floyd has just observed that Jack and Liz are acting like they're dating.
jokes.punchline: Liz, flustered and deflecting, blurts out a non-sequitur agreement with Ann Coulter as a conversation-ender.
jokes.explanation: A beautiful awkward deflection. Liz, a liberal, is so desperate to change the subject she accidentally agrees with Ann Coulter. The specificity (not just 'a conservative commentator' but Coulter) and the utter randomness of the timing make this a great Liz Lemon moment. Strong character integration — her social awkwardness under pressure is perfectly captured.

jokes.text: Oh, he took his kids to that Russian cat circus.
jokes.setup: Someone asks where Pete is.
jokes.punchline: Pete is at a Russian cat circus — delivered as a totally unremarkable fact.
jokes.explanation: Throwaway absurdist detail that works entirely because of its casualness. 'Russian cat circus' is specific enough to be funny, and Liz's total nonchalance makes it a great background world-building joke.

jokes.text: The extended writers' room dancing/rap video scene — writers in an empty office doing old school hip-hop moves, mentioning a humidifier, a used Kleenex, Kid 'n Play, Davy Jones.
jokes.setup: The writers' room appears to be having a full dance party with 'old school' hip-hop moves.
jokes.punchline: The mundane details (humidifier, used Kleenex, VapoRub) are inserted into what sounds like a rap video parody, making the contrast between the aspirational genre and the sad reality the joke.
jokes.explanation: Extended absurdist sequence that works through accumulation. The VapoRub line ('this VapoRub isn't gonna get under my nose by itself') is the standout moment within it — the writers living their worst lives while trying to be cool. Runs slightly long.

jokes.text: 'Cause this VapoRub isn't gonna get under my nose by itself.
jokes.setup: Floyd suggests not going out to meet Jack
jokes.punchline: Liz's reason for staying home is VapoRub under her nose — her version of a sexy night in involves cold medicine
jokes.explanation: One of Liz Lemon's defining character jokes. Her romantic evening involves VapoRub self-application — it's simultaneously sad, specific, and completely her. 'Isn't gonna get under my nose by itself' has the structure of a self-important statement applied to the most deflating possible action. Justifies 8+.

jokes.text: Floyd's phone texting exchange with Jack: Jack texts 'Good night' / 'And sleep tight' / 'And don't let the bed...' / 'All right, enough. Give me that.'
jokes.setup: Floyd's phone keeps getting Jack texts in the middle of the night.
jokes.punchline: Jack is texting the classic bedtime rhyme to Floyd in installments, treating midnight texting to Liz's boyfriend as normal — and gets three-quarters through 'don't let the bedbugs bite' before Liz takes the phone.
jokes.explanation: Beautifully escalating joke. Jack texting Floyd at midnight is already overstepping. The content being a nursery rhyme sent in three separate texts is wonderfully absurd. The structure — three successive messages building toward an interrupted punchline — is tight. Jack's possessiveness over Floyd has escalated to bedtime rituals.

jokes.text: Jack, I have taken a sleeping pill because I have a big lawyer meeting... / That's what we call them. / ...in the morning. Floyd.
jokes.setup: Liz grabs Floyd's phone and reads Jack's text back; it's a formal, almost business-letter response.
jokes.punchline: Floyd has written a formal sign-off ('Floyd.') to his midnight bedtime-rhyme text, and 'that's what we call them' implies there's a category called 'big lawyer meetings.'
jokes.explanation: Floyd signing off a text with 'Floyd.' like a formal letter is very funny, especially in a midnight context. 'That's what we call them' adds a conspiratorial layer. Good character work for Floyd — he's adapting Jack's business formality into personal life.

jokes.text: 'Lemon, is that you?' / 'I always sign it Floydster.'
jokes.setup: Liz has responded to Jack's text and Jack texts back thinking it's Floyd.
jokes.punchline: Liz claims to have Floyd's signature nickname — 'Floydster' — a callback to Jack stealing the nickname Liz objected to earlier.
jokes.explanation: Good callback — Liz denied Jack the nickname 'Floydster' earlier, and here she's using it herself while pretending to BE Floyd. The joke reveals she's adopted the nickname she forbade Jack to use. Nice character consistency.

jokes.text: Oh, it's Jack. / Don't answer it. [lights off, get down]
jokes.setup: Jack calls their apartment phone after the texts.
jokes.punchline: Liz and Floyd turn off the lights and hide from Jack — treating a phone call from a colleague as a home invasion threat.
jokes.explanation: 'The call is coming from inside the house' is a great horror-movie reference delivered as if Jack is a genuine threat. The absurdity of adults hiding in the dark from a phone call escalates Jack's intrusion into their relationship to absurd stakes.

jokes.text: The call is coming from inside the house. / All right, turn off the lights and get down.
jokes.setup: Liz and Floyd are hiding from Jack's phone call in the dark.
jokes.punchline: Liz deploys the classic horror-movie phrase 'the call is coming from inside the house' — meaning Jack is literally in their building.
jokes.explanation: Horror-movie reference repurposed for Jack's romantic rivalry. 'All right, turn off the lights and get down' after the horror reference perfectly commits to the bit — they're treating Jack as a slasher villain. The phrase itself is very quotable.

jokes.text: Jack arrives at the window / 'Oh, my God.' / 'Can he see us?' / 'The call is coming from inside the house.' / 'All right, turn off the lights and get down.'
jokes.setup: Liz and Floyd are hiding from Jack's calls
jokes.punchline: 'The call is coming from inside the house' — a horror movie reference that's perfectly deployed when Jack apparently appears at or near their window
jokes.explanation: The horror movie reference ('When a Stranger Calls') deployed for Jack's stalker-like appearance is genuinely inspired. The escalation from hiding from phone calls to turning off lights and getting down is great physical comedy even in transcript form. Strong joke that earns its horror-reference shorthand.

jokes.text: He tried to drop them off at your house last night, but someone pretended not to be home.
jokes.setup: Jonathan gives Liz Knicks tickets from Jack, noting he tried to deliver them the night before.
jokes.punchline: Jonathan matter-of-factly calls out that Liz hid from Jack — 'pretended not to be home' — revealing Jack knew all along.
jokes.explanation: Callback that pays off the hiding-in-the-dark scene by revealing it was futile — Jack knew. Jonathan delivering this as a simple fact with no judgment is perfectly deadpan. The beat confirms Jack's omniscience, which ties back to the 'turning around without turning around' joke.

jokes.text: And you, of course. [said as an afterthought]
jokes.setup: Jonathan says Jack 'seems very taken with Floyd.'
jokes.punchline: He adds 'And you, of course' as an afterthought, making it clear Liz is an afterthought compared to Floyd in Jack's affections.
jokes.explanation: The 'of course' as an afterthought is a well-timed dagger. Jonathan's deadpan delivery of the obvious insult to Liz without any malice is very funny. Good economy — the joke lives in the pause before 'And you, of course.'

jokes.text: ...inventor... / I shall call it 'Susan.'
jokes.setup: The trailer describes Jefferson as an inventor.
jokes.punchline: Jefferson names his invention 'Susan' — which is both historically wrong and completely anticlimactic (Jefferson invented many things, none named Susan).
jokes.explanation: Perfect throwaway absurdist punchline within the trailer sequence. 'I shall call it Susan' is funny precisely because it's a flat, generic name dropped with Founding Father gravitas. The non-specificity (of what the invention even is) adds to it.

jokes.text: ...Jungle Fever-Haver. / I am with child. What? / Will you free me and make me your wife? / Um, I'm gonna have to get back to you on that.
jokes.setup: The trailer describes Jefferson as a 'Jungle Fever-Haver' and shows the Hemings relationship.
jokes.punchline: Tracy (playing both Jefferson AND Hemings) has a scene where he tells himself he is with child, and then responds to his own marriage proposal with 'I'm gonna have to get back to you on that' — Jefferson's actual historical non-answer.
jokes.explanation: Episode highlight. Tracy playing both Jefferson AND Hemings means he's having a scene with himself where he proposes to himself. 'Jungle Fever-Haver' as a screen credit is brilliantly irreverent. 'I'm gonna have to get back to you on that' as Jefferson's response to a marriage proposal is historically pointed AND perfectly characterizes the evasion. Only Tracy Jordan makes this joke work. Extremely quotable.

jokes.text: Source Award nominee Tracy Jordan... / NAACP Image Award presenter Tracy Jordan... / and Academy Award watcher Tracy Jordan is... Jefferson.
jokes.setup: The trailer presents Tracy's credentials as the star.
jokes.punchline: His credits escalate downward: from award nominee → award presenter → award WATCHER — the final credit being simply that he has observed an awards ceremony.
jokes.explanation: Episode's best joke. A perfectly structured three-step descending escalation: nominee → presenter → WATCHER. Each step is lower than the last, and 'watcher' is the inspired final humiliation — his greatest achievement is having attended the ceremony. The structure is airtight, the concept is original, the character integration is perfect (only Tracy Jordan's credits would descend this specifically), and the economy is excellent. This is comparable to the Snip-Snap reference level — a culturally specific joke that lands perfectly. Close to a 9.0.

jokes.text: This is for you, Don Geiss. [Tracy, in costume, breaking the fourth wall to dedicate the trailer]
jokes.setup: The Jefferson trailer reaches its climax.
jokes.punchline: Tracy breaks from the trailer to speak directly to Geiss — 'This is for you, Don Geiss' — as if dedicating a film to an executive who hasn't greenlit it.
jokes.explanation: Tracy dedicating the trailer mid-trailer to the man he's trying to impress is a good meta-moment. The earnestness is the joke. Good character integration.

jokes.text: Well, Tracy... that was terrible. The answer is 'no.'
jokes.setup: After watching the full Jefferson trailer, Geiss gives his verdict.
jokes.punchline: Geiss's response is two brutally direct sentences — no qualifier, no softening. 'That was terrible.' Full stop.
jokes.explanation: The brevity and finality of 'That was terrible. The answer is no.' after all that buildup is perfect comedy deflation. Economy is nearly maxed. Geiss's flat authority makes this work — no hedging, no emotion. The contrast with the epic trailer is the joke.

jokes.text: The champagne cork/cabin pressure story: 'I don't give a damn about the masks. I'm on all fours trying to shove the corks back in the bottles.'
jokes.setup: Jack tells the story of sitting next to Don Geiss on a plane and trying to make a good impression when the cabin pressure drops.
jokes.punchline: His instinct during an aircraft emergency is to protect the expensive champagne — oxygen masks mean nothing compared to the bottles.
jokes.explanation: A great Jack story. The inversion — treating champagne corks as more important than oxygen masks during an emergency — is a perfect encapsulation of Jack's value system. 'I don't give a damn about the masks' is the punchline word-for-word. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: And Don Geiss says, 'Now, there's an executive who knows how to keep his costs down.'
jokes.setup: Jack describes crawling on the plane floor saving champagne corks during an emergency.
jokes.punchline: Geiss interprets Jack's cork-saving behavior not as eccentric or dangerous but as admirable fiscal responsibility.
jokes.explanation: The punchline of the champagne story — Geiss rewarding Jack for mid-emergency cost-consciousness — reveals both characters perfectly. Two executives whose values are so aligned that this behavior earns admiration rather than alarm. The specificity of 'keeps his costs down' as the takeaway is perfectly absurd.

jokes.text: No. Lemon, you're the third wheel. / Men seek out the company of other men they admire and want to be like. Floyd is me 20 years ago. I'm Don Geiss 30 years ago.
jokes.setup: Liz tells Jack he's being a third wheel at the Knicks game.
jokes.punchline: Jack reframes the entire social dynamic — he's not the interloper, Liz is, because men form aspirational chains of mentorship while women are superfluous to this structure.
jokes.explanation: Jack's theory of male bonding as a succession chain (Floyd→Jack→Geiss) is both satirically accurate and beautifully absurd. The fact that he's worked this all out and presents it as inarguable fact is perfect Jack. The logic is internally consistent which makes it funnier.

jokes.text: 20 years from now, Floyd will be me, I'm gonna be Don Geiss, and Don Geiss will be dead.
jokes.setup: Jack is laying out his theory of male succession.
jokes.punchline: The logical conclusion of the succession chain — Don Geiss being dead — delivered as a neutral fact in the same tone as the rest.
jokes.explanation: A pitch-perfect escalation punchline. The succession chain leads inevitably to 'and Don Geiss will be dead' — delivered with the same businesslike tone as the rest. The dark matter-of-factness (not said with malice or sadness) is very Jack. Great economy, strong character integration. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor.

jokes.text: Not that I blame you, because I could take him away from you if I wanted to.
jokes.setup: Liz tells Jack to back off her boyfriend.
jokes.punchline: Jack's response to being told to back off is to threaten to steal Floyd — delivered as a reasonable caveat, not a threat.
jokes.explanation: Jack casually threatening to steal Liz's boyfriend while making it sound like he's being magnanimous is excellent character work. The calm delivery of what is an enormous threat makes it funnier.

jokes.text: How about some kind of time-share arrangement? You can have him Monday, Wednesday, and Friday. / I don't want Friday. We have a show.
jokes.setup: The Jack-Floyd-Liz dynamic has been compared to a love triangle.
jokes.punchline: Jack proposes a time-share arrangement for Floyd. Liz's counter isn't 'no' but 'not Friday' — she's actually engaging with the terms.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. Jack proposing a time-share for a person is absurd enough. But Liz responding to the specifics ('I don't want Friday. We have a show.') rather than rejecting the premise reveals she's accepted his framing — she's negotiating days. The fact that her reason for not wanting Friday is professional, not personal, is the topper. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: All right. How about some kind of a time-share arrangement? You can have him Monday, Wednesday, and Friday.
jokes.setup: Liz says Jack can't use Floyd to feel better about himself
jokes.punchline: Jack proposes a formal time-share schedule for Floyd — treating a human being's companionship as a real estate agreement
jokes.explanation: Applying corporate/real estate negotiation to human friendship is peak Jack Donaghy. The specific offer of Mon/Wed/Fri shows he's thought about the schedule. Justifies 8.

jokes.text: Look at your life, Jack. It's like this skybox. It's fancy and it's empty and it smells like crab cakes.
jokes.setup: Liz confronts Jack about using Floyd to feel better about himself.
jokes.punchline: Her metaphor for Jack's life is the empty, crab-cake-smelling skybox — the 'crab cakes' detail transforming a decent observation into something funnier and more specific.
jokes.explanation: 'Fancy and empty and smells like crab cakes' is a beautifully specific three-part metaphor. The first two qualities are emotionally resonant, and 'smells like crab cakes' is the unexpected physical detail that turns it from sincere to funny. Liz at her best — genuinely insightful but unable to resist the absurd detail.

jokes.text: Then he offered me $7 million to reprise my role as Cocoa the Dog.
jokes.setup: Tracy reports that Geiss said no to Jefferson
jokes.punchline: The callback reveals that Tracy has played a character called 'Cocoa the Dog' — presumably related to the Fat Bitch universe — for $7 million
jokes.explanation: The 'Cocoa the Dog' credit expands the 'Fat Bitch' universe absurdly. The $7 million specificity is funny — it's a precise, real offer for an absurd role.

jokes.text: ß I'm gonna get an iPhone ß / ß Everybody's gonna be jealous ß
jokes.setup: Tracy has just been rejected by Geiss and offered $7 million to do 'Fat Bitch 2.'
jokes.punchline: He sings an impromptu song about getting an iPhone — apparently this is how he processes being offered $7 million.
jokes.explanation: Tracy spontaneously singing about an iPhone as an emotional response to rejection is perfectly on-brand absurdism. The non-sequitur nature of it — $7 million → iPhone — shows Tracy's complete inability to prioritize conventionally.

jokes.text: No, I turned him down. / It's like a roller-coaster ride of emotion in here.
jokes.setup: Tracy says he turned down the $7 million deal.
jokes.punchline: Kenneth describes his own experience watching Tracy as a 'roller-coaster ride of emotion' — his comment is about witnessing Tracy, not about what Tracy just said.
jokes.explanation: Kenneth's emotional response to watching Tracy is a good character beat. The understatement of 'roller-coaster ride of emotion' for what has included iPhones, horse defecation, and Thomas Jefferson is well-placed.

jokes.text: Your first order of business... Get that dead horse out of my car.
jokes.setup: Tracy gives Kenneth his first assignment as someone who will help finance his movie.
jokes.punchline: The horse (Caractacus) is now dead and is in Tracy's car — revealed completely casually.
jokes.explanation: Perfect dark callback. The horse from the office (Caractacus) has died and ended up in Tracy's car. The escalation of horse-related problems (wig eaten → erection → crapping in office → dead in car) is a great running bit. The casual delivery — 'Get that dead horse out of my car' as a first order of business — is excellent. The specificity (Tracy's car, not just 'somewhere') makes it funnier.

jokes.text: I'm having terrible Lemon problems. I'm eating all the time. I mean, who eats 16 flautas after midnight?
jokes.setup: Jack is confiding in Phoebe about his problems.
jokes.punchline: His 'Lemon problems' manifest as stress-eating 16 flautas after midnight — the specific number (16) and the specific food (flautas) make it.
jokes.explanation: The specificity is everything — '16 flautas' rather than 'a lot of food,' after midnight rather than 'late.' Jack Donaghy stress-eating 16 flautas is a beautifully absurd image. Strong character integration — only Jack would frame personal problems as 'Lemon problems' as if Liz is a category of malfunction.

jokes.text: Listen, if you're still interested, there is another piece I'd like to show you... that you might enjoy. / I'll need to take you back to the private office. / This piece is very delicate. / Very few people have handled it. / Oh, God, I hope we're talking about the same thing.
jokes.setup: Phoebe tells Jack there's another art piece she'd like to show him, using art-handling language.
jokes.punchline: Jack's response — 'Oh, God, I hope we're talking about the same thing' — recontextualizes every preceding line as either about art or about sex, without resolving which.
jokes.explanation: Classic double entendre escalation, with Phoebe's art language becoming increasingly interpretable as sexual. Jack's punchline ('I hope we're talking about the same thing') is the perfect cap — it implies he's not sure which conversation they're having and doesn't care. The earnestness of both readings makes it work.

jokes.text: Will you marry me? / No. / The ruby-diamond cluster. / I bought it back from the anonymous Arab.
jokes.setup: Jack proposes marriage to Phoebe. She says no.
jokes.punchline: He then produces the ring — his ex-wife's engagement ring, which he sold to an anonymous buyer at the start of the episode — meaning he bought back his own ex-wife's engagement ring to propose to a new woman.
jokes.explanation: Excellent full-episode callback and structural payoff. The engagement ring established in the Christie's scene returns as the proposal ring — Jack bought back his ex-wife's ring to propose to a new woman within hours of meeting her. The layers: (1) he hated Bianca, (2) he sold her ring, (3) he bought it back, (4) he proposes with it immediately. Phoebe's instant 'No' before seeing the ring is the first beat; the ring reveal is the second. Very well-constructed.

jokes.text: The ruby-diamond cluster. I bought it back from the anonymous Arab.
jokes.setup: Jack proposes with a ring
jokes.punchline: He's bought back Bianca's engagement ring — the same ring that was used to buy a boat named 'Bianca Blows' that was sunk — now repurposed for Phoebe
jokes.explanation: Excellent multi-callback. The engagement ring that sold to an 'anonymous Arab,' funded a boat called 'The Bianca Blows' that Phoebe sank, is now back in Jack's hands for a new proposal. The circularity is delightfully convoluted. 'Bought it back from the anonymous Arab' is the specific phrase that makes it land.

jokes.text: How romantic. / Ow. // I'm sorry. / It's okay. // Ow. // Careful, my bones.
jokes.setup: Jack puts the engagement ring on Phoebe's finger after she's accepted (off-screen).
jokes.punchline: Her 'avian bone syndrome' means the ring hurts her finger — 'Careful, my bones' — the running gag pays off in the most tender possible way.
jokes.explanation: Beautiful callback payoff. The 'avian bone syndrome' gag established at their first meeting returns as the final beat of their engagement — the ring hurts her hollow bones. The joke structure (romantic moment → pain → 'careful, my bones') is both funny and weirdly touching. Jack having found someone whose bones require careful handling is absurdly perfect for him.

tmdb_overview: The tables have turned inside 30 Rock: Liz is actually happy in her new relationship with Floyd while Jack finds his job may be in jeopardy after his televised fireworks fiasco prompts top GE man Don Geiss to warn he's got his eye on Jack's performance. Tracy vies for Geiss' attention, hoping to turn his feature film idea for Jefferson into a reality.
insight: Observational comedy sustains 77.8 score despite thin standout moments across 62 jokes.
